reason: The provided sources offer 16 cross-verified claims from at least five distinct websites, covering the commonality, extreme lifespans, and planetary habits of red dwarf stars.
story: Myth: The Sun is a typical star. Busted: Our Sun is actually a rare monster. Up to 80% of stars in the Milky Way are red dwarfs—tiny, dim embers that make the Sun look like a giant. Even our closest neighbor, Proxima Centauri, is one, yet you can’t see it. In fact, not a single red dwarf is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye from Earth. These are the universe’s ultimate marathon runners; while the Sun dies in billions of years, red dwarfs can live for trillions. Not a single one has ever died in the history of the universe. They recycle their fuel through convection, mixing helium through their entire bodies to keep the fire going. They often host Earth-sized worlds, but there’s a twist: these planets are likely tidally locked, trapped in eternal day or frozen night.
angle: Not a single red dwarf is visible to the naked eye, despite making up 80% of all stars in the Milky Way.

claims.claim: Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in our galaxy.
Red dwarfs comprise between 75% and 80% of all stars in the Milky Way.
No red dwarf star is bright enough to be visible to the unaided human eye from Earth.
Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf and is the nearest star to the Sun.
Red dwarfs are the smallest, coolest, and least massive stars on the main sequence.
These stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
Red dwarf lifespans are estimated to reach into the trillions of years.
No red dwarf has yet reached an advanced stage of evolution because the universe is not old enough.
Smallest red dwarfs are fully convective, meaning they mix fuel throughout their entire interior.
Convection in low-mass red dwarfs prevents helium from accumulating in the core by constantly remixing it.
Many red dwarfs are flare stars that can double their brightness in mere minutes.
Red dwarfs often host Earth-sized or potentially habitable planets.
Habitable zone planets orbiting red dwarfs are likely tidally locked, with one side always facing the star.
Red dwarfs are predicted to eventually shrink and evolve into white dwarfs.
Red dwarfs are scientifically categorized as M-class or M dwarfs.
To be potentially habitable, planets must orbit a red dwarf much closer than Mercury orbits the Sun.

disputed: The total percentage of stars that are red dwarfs is cited as 75% according to one account and 80% according to another.
The exact mass limit for full convection varies between 0.35 and 0.4 solar masses depending on the stellar model.
Estimates for red dwarf lifespans vary widely, from 80 billion years in one report to trillions of years in others.
Proxima Centauri's radius is described as 9% of the Sun's radius in one source and one-seventh (approx 14%) of its diameter in another.
The final evolution state of low-mass red dwarfs is variously described as becoming a white dwarf or eventually a black dwarf.
The habitability of tidally locked worlds is debated; while some suggest atmospheric freeze-out is a risk, others cite models where heat circulation maintains liquid water.
